--- title: "HW 08: Should Jo Make the Drive?" author: "Insert Name Here" subtitle: "Running the experiment and analyzing it with multiple regression" editor: visual format: html: embed-resources: true include-in-header: text: | --- # Introduction In HW 07 you planned an experiment for Jo: you worked out how many extra cups Jo needs to sell at City Hall to cover the gas, turned that into an effect size, and used a power analysis to decide how many days Jo needs to run the experiment. In this HW you **run the experiment** and analyze it with **multiple linear regression**. Why multiple regression? The temperature changes from shift to shift, Jo can't control it, and it probably affects how much coffee people buy. If we put `Temperature` in the model alongside `Location`, we can ask whether City Hall is better *holding the temperature constant*, and we might get a more precise answer than with `Location` alone. ::: callout-note This is an **individual** assignment, but you're welcome to talk through ideas with classmates. Your code and writing should be your own. Each of you will collect your own data, so your numbers will differ from your classmates' numbers. ::: ## Learning goals By the end of this homework, you will... - Carry out an experiment you planned with a power analysis - Fit a multiple linear regression with a categorical and a quantitative predictor, and interpret each coefficient "holding the other predictor constant" - Explain why adding a predictor can change a coefficient and its standard error - Visualize an additive model as parallel lines - Weigh an estimate against a practical break-even point, and use it, along with a p-value, to make a recommendation - Distinguish association from causation in a regression # Getting Started ### Log in to RStudio - Go to [RStudio](https://rstudio.collegeofidaho.edu/) and login with your College of Idaho Email and Password. - Use the `hw` folder you made earlier in the semester. Create a subfolder called `hw08` to store this homework. - Log into [Canvas](https://cofi.instructure.com/courses/18743), navigate to HW-08, and download the `hw-08.qmd` file. Upload it into the folder you just made. ## R and RStudio See the [R resources](https://ericfriedlander.github.io/math2025-fa26/computing-r-resources.html) page for a guide to the RStudio IDE and Quarto file components. # Packages We will use the following packages in this HW. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) library(ggformula) library(broom) library(knitr) ``` ::: # The Coffee Truck, one more time Here is Jo's question from HW 07 again. Jo normally parks the truck in the **Business District** for both the **Morning** and **Lunch** shifts, and is wondering whether it would be better to leave the Business District after the Morning shift and drive to **City Hall** for Lunch instead. The drive costs **\$15 in gas** each day Jo makes it, and Jo charges **\$3 per cup**, so moving only pays off if Jo sells enough extra cups at City Hall to cover the gas. The experiment: each day, Jo randomly chooses whether to spend Lunch in the Business District or at City Hall. The response is the number of cups sold during the Lunch shift (`Sales`). This time the game also records the `Temperature` (in °F) during the shift. Jo does not control it. # Exercises ::: callout-tip Write all code and narrative in your Quarto file. Write all narrative in complete sentences. Throughout the assignment, you should periodically **render** your Quarto document to produce the updated HTML file. Make sure we can read all of your code in your HTML file. This means you will need to break up long lines of code. One way to help avoid long lines of code is to start a new line after every pipe (`|>`). In your `hw-08.qmd` document you'll see that each task is wrapped in an `exercise` box, with an empty `answer` box below it for you to fill in your response. Use this format for the remaining exercises. ::: ## Part 1: Run the experiment ::::: exercise **Collect and load your data.** In HW 07 you planned an experiment. Now run it. a. **Recap your plan.** Open your `hw-07.qmd` and state each of the following in a sentence in the answer box: the break-even number of extra cups at City Hall (from \$15 of gas at \$3 per cup), $\hat{\sigma}_\epsilon$ (your estimate of the day-to-day noise), the effect size $d$ Jo needs to detect, and the number of days per location that gives 80% power. b. Go to the [Coffee Truck game](https://www.stat2games.sites.grinnell.edu/games/coffeetruck.html). On the ID screen, enter **`MATH2025FA26`** as the Group Name and enter your Team Name. ::: callout-important This game's data lands in a table that's **public to anyone**, attached to your group name. Pick a team name that doesn't identify you. ::: c. Set up your sim: - **Location**: select `Business` and `CityHall`. - **Time Of Day**: select `Lunch` only. - **Price**: \$3. **Music**: none. - **Design Type**: `Random Sample`. The game plays the combinations in a random order, which plays the role of the coin flip from HW 07. - The game asks for **repetitions**, not days. One repetition is one combination of the settings you chose. You chose two locations and one level of everything else, so each repetition is **two days**: one at each location. - Use the **minimum** number of repetitions that gives at least your planned number of days per location. Check that the game reports the number of days you expect before you start. - The game limits how many repetitions you can run. If you can't reach your planned number, use the maximum the game allows. d. Click **Start Sim**, then `Get All Sales Data` -\> `Continue` -\> `Game Data`. Enter **`MATH2025FA26`** for your group name and your Team Name in the PlayerID field. e. Download the CSV, rename it `coffee-hw08.csv`, and upload it to your `data` folder. f. Read it into R with `read_csv()` in the chunk below, and write one or two sentences about how you set up the experiment, including how many days you ran and whether it matches your power analysis. ::::: ::: answer ::: {.cell} ::: ::: ::: callout-note If the game isn't working, ask me for the class data set instead. It has fewer days than your power analysis called for, so say so in your write-up. ::: ::: exercise **Check your data.** Use `glimpse()` to check the columns and `count()` to see how many days you got at each `Location`. - Did you get close to your planned number of days at each location? Why are the counts equal (or nearly equal) here, unlike in a coin-flip design? - What range of `Temperature` did you see at each location? (Hint: `group_by()` and `summarize()`.) ::: ::: answer ::: {.cell} ::: ::: ## Part 2: The analysis you planned ::: exercise Make a boxplot of `Sales` by `Location`. Then make a scatterplot of `Sales` vs. `Temperature` with the points colored by `Location`. Describe what you see. Does `Temperature` look different at the two locations? ::: ::: answer ::: {.cell} ::: ::: ::: exercise Fit the simple linear regression you planned in HW 07: `Sales ~ Location`. Save it as `fit_loc` and display it with `tidy()` and `glance()`. - What is the reference level? Interpret the `Location` coefficient in context. - Compare the estimate to your break-even from Exercise 1. Is it bigger or smaller? Is it statistically significant? ::: ::: answer ::: {.cell} ::: ::: ## Part 3: Adding temperature ::: exercise Fit a multiple linear regression of `Sales` on `Location` **and** `Temperature` and save it as `fit_both`. Display it with `tidy()`. Write the fitted equation (using an indicator variable for `Location`) and interpret **every** coefficient in context. Use the phrase "holding ... constant" for the slopes. Is the intercept meaningful here? ::: ::: answer ::: {.cell} ::: ::: ::: exercise Compare `fit_loc` and `fit_both`. Use `tidy()` and `glance()` to find the numbers, then fill in the markdown table template in your answer box (round to 2 decimal places, and use 4 for the p-values). Then answer: a. Did the `Location` coefficient change much? Why or why not? (Hint: look at your answer to Exercise 3.) b. Did $\hat{\sigma}_\epsilon$ go up or down when you added `Temperature`? What happened to the standard error of the `Location` coefficient? Why does this matter for detecting the effect of moving? ::: ::: answer ::: {.cell} ::: | | `fit_loc` (`Location` only) | `fit_both` (`Location` + `Temperature`) | |:----------------------------------|:-------:|:-------:| | `Location` coefficient (`LocationCityHall`) | | | | Std. error of the `Location` coefficient | | | | p-value of the `Location` coefficient | | | | $\hat{\sigma}_\epsilon$ (`sigma`) | | | | $R^2$ | | | ::: ::: exercise Use `augment()` on `fit_both` to plot the data as points and the fitted values as lines, with both colored by `Location`. What do you notice about the lines? What does that mean about the difference between the two locations at a cold day compared to a hot day? Is that assumption believable? ::: ::: answer ::: {.cell} ::: ::: ## Part 4: Should Jo make the drive? ::: exercise **The bottom line in dollars.** a. Use `predict()` with `fit_both` to predict `Sales` at each location on a day with the **mean** `Temperature` from your data. Subtract to get the predicted difference in cups, and check that it matches the `Location` coefficient. b. Convert that difference into dollars: how much extra revenue does City Hall bring in per day, and how much is left after the \$15 of gas? c. Each cup also costs Jo about \$1 in ingredients, so Jo only keeps \$2 per cup. Redo the calculation. How much does Jo gain or lose per day by driving to City Hall? ::: ::: answer ::: {.cell} ::: ::: ::: exercise **Make a recommendation.** Write a short paragraph (4 to 6 sentences) for Jo that answers: **is it better to switch to City Hall for Lunch?** Your paragraph should address: - the estimated extra cups at City Hall (holding `Temperature` constant) compared to the break-even, and the dollars Jo gains or loses per day - the p-value. Remember that it tests whether the true difference is *zero*, not whether it exceeds the break-even. - how precise the estimate is: how big is the `std.error` relative to the gap between the estimate and the break-even? - whether the result is statistically significant, practically significant, both, or neither, and what you would tell Jo to do ::: ::: answer ::: ::: exercise **Reflection.** a. In HW 07 you chose the number of days to get 80% power to detect the break-even effect. Suppose your `Location` coefficient is below the break-even and not statistically significant. Does that mean City Hall is no better than the Business District? Use the power analysis in your answer. b. Jo randomly assigned `Location`, but did not assign `Temperature`. Can Jo claim that moving to City Hall *causes* the change in sales? Can Jo claim that a warmer day *causes* the change in sales associated with `Temperature`? Explain the difference. c. Jo's friend says, "Temperature is a distraction. Just use `Sales ~ Location`." Based on your results, do you agree? Why or why not? ::: ::: answer ::: ::: callout-tip You're done and ready to submit your work! Render your document and upload the .qmd and .html files to Canvas. ::: # Grading (30 pts + 2 pts for writing and workflow)
